question: Did ancients believe in free will?

positions.label: Determinism
positions.summary: Fate governs all things through an unbreakable chain of causes
positions.key_argument: If anything could happen uncaused, the universe would be chaotic

positions.label: Libertarian Free Will
positions.summary: The atomic swerve allows genuine choice free from determinism
positions.key_argument: Moral responsibility requires genuine alternatives

corpus_verdict: Determinism dominates in philosophical texts, but literary texts often assume genuine choice
temporal_trend: Compatibilism grows from 15% (Hellenistic) to 35% (Imperial) as Stoics and Platonists synthesize
genre_effect: Philosophy splits evenly; tragedy strongly favors determinism; rhetoric assumes free will

question: What happens to the soul after death?

positions.label: Immortal Soul
positions.summary: The soul is immortal and continues existence in a spiritual realm
positions.key_argument: The soul's ability to know eternal truths proves its immortal nature

positions.label: Mortality
positions.summary: The soul dissolves at death; consciousness ceases completely
positions.key_argument: Soul is atomic composition that disperses when the body dies

positions.label: Underworld Existence
positions.summary: Souls exist as shades in Hades, retaining some consciousness
positions.key_argument: The dead can be contacted and retain memories of life

corpus_verdict: Philosophical texts lean toward immortality; poetry maintains traditional underworld beliefs
temporal_trend: Immortality doctrine strengthens from 25% (Archaic) to 45% (Late Imperial) with Christian influence
genre_effect: Epic poetry preserves underworld tradition; philosophy debates immortality vs mortality

question: What is the nature of women?

positions.label: Natural Inferiority
positions.summary: Women are naturally inferior in reason and should be subordinate
positions.key_argument: Female is a deformed male, lacking full rational capacity

positions.label: Equal Potential
positions.summary: Women have equal rational capacity when properly educated
positions.key_argument: Virtue is the same in men and women; only training differs

positions.label: Complementary Roles
positions.summary: Men and women have different but complementary natural roles
positions.key_argument: Nature assigns distinct functions that benefit the whole

corpus_verdict: Inferiority doctrine dominates across genres, with rare challenges in philosophical texts
temporal_trend: Complementary view grows from 10% (Classical) to 25% (Imperial) with Stoic influence
genre_effect: Philosophy occasionally questions assumptions; medicine reinforces inferiority; law codifies subordination

question: Is slavery naturally justified?

positions.label: Natural Slavery
positions.summary: Some humans are naturally suited for slavery due to inferior reason
positions.key_argument: Natural hierarchy exists; some benefit from being ruled by superiors

positions.label: Conventional Institution
positions.summary: Slavery is social convention, not natural; all humans share reason
positions.key_argument: The mind cannot be enslaved; external conditions don't affect inner freedom

positions.label: Complete Rejection
positions.summary: Slavery violates natural equality of all humans
positions.key_argument: God made no one a slave; all humans are naturally free

corpus_verdict: Natural justification predominates, with Stoic conventional view gaining influence
temporal_trend: Conventional view grows from 20% (Classical) to 40% (Imperial) through Stoic influence
genre_effect: Philosophy debates justification; legal texts assume legitimacy; comedy satirizes relations

question: Do gods intervene in human affairs?

positions.label: Active Intervention
positions.summary: Gods regularly intervene to help favorites and punish offenders
positions.key_argument: Historical events and personal experiences show divine action

positions.label: Non-Intervention
positions.summary: Gods exist but remain completely detached from human affairs
positions.key_argument: Divine happiness requires freedom from human concerns and emotions

positions.label: Providential Order
positions.summary: Divine reason guides the universe but through natural law, not arbitrary intervention
positions.key_argument: Cosmic order shows rational divine planning without caprice

corpus_verdict: Traditional intervention belief dominates literature; philosophy splits between providence and non-intervention
temporal_trend: Providential view grows from 15% (Classical) to 35% (Imperial) with Platonic revival
genre_effect: Epic and history assume intervention; philosophy debates mechanism; tragedy shows divine justice

question: Is democracy or monarchy the best government?

positions.label: Democracy
positions.summary: Rule by the people ensures freedom and prevents tyranny
positions.key_argument: Collective wisdom surpasses individual judgment; equality is natural right

positions.label: Monarchy
positions.summary: Rule by the best individual ensures efficient and wise governance
positions.key_argument: Unity of command and expertise of the ruler produce optimal decisions

positions.label: Mixed Constitution
positions.summary: Combination of democratic, aristocratic, and monarchical elements
positions.key_argument: Each form checks the others' weaknesses; stability through balance

corpus_verdict: Monarchy slightly favored in theoretical texts; democracy praised in Athenian sources
temporal_trend: Mixed constitution gains from 15% (Classical) to 40% (Hellenistic-Roman) after Alexander
genre_effect: Political theory favors mixed forms; oratory praises democracy; history shows monarchy's effectiveness

question: Should pleasure or virtue be life's goal?

positions.label: Pleasure as Highest Good
positions.summary: Pleasure is the natural goal; virtue is valuable only as means to pleasure
positions.key_argument: All animals naturally seek pleasure and avoid pain; this reveals nature's intent

positions.label: Virtue as Highest Good
positions.summary: Virtue alone constitutes the good life; pleasure is indifferent or corrupting
positions.key_argument: Virtue alone is under our control and makes us godlike

positions.label: Virtue and Pleasure Combined
positions.summary: The good life requires both virtue and moderate pleasure
positions.key_argument: Human flourishing involves rational activity accompanied by appropriate pleasure

corpus_verdict: Virtue tradition dominates philosophical discourse; pleasure philosophy influential in private life
temporal_trend: Combined view grows from 20% (Hellenistic) to 30% (Imperial) as systems synthesize
genre_effect: Philosophy debates the issue extensively; poetry often celebrates pleasure; biography praises virtue

question: Is Greek or Roman culture superior?

positions.label: Greek Superiority
positions.summary: Greek culture excels in philosophy, arts, and intellectual achievement
positions.key_argument: Greeks invented philosophy and democracy; Romans merely copy and conquer

positions.label: Roman Superiority
positions.summary: Roman culture excels in practical governance, law, and moral character
positions.key_argument: Roman virtue and discipline created lasting empire; Greek cleverness breeds instability

positions.label: Complementary Excellence
positions.summary: Greeks excel in theory and arts, Romans in practice and governance
positions.key_argument: Rome's destiny is to rule; Greece's gift is wisdom and beauty

corpus_verdict: Roman sources claim superiority while borrowing heavily; Greek sources maintain cultural pride
temporal_trend: Complementary view grows from 15% (Republican) to 30% (Imperial) as cultures blend
genre_effect: Roman history and oratory claim superiority; philosophy acknowledges Greek precedence

question: Does fate control human destiny?

positions.label: Absolute Fate
positions.summary: All events are predetermined; human action cannot alter destiny
positions.key_argument: The web of causation is unbreakable; even gods cannot change fate

positions.label: Human Agency
positions.summary: Humans have genuine power to shape their future through choice
positions.key_argument: Deliberation and regret prove we have real alternatives

positions.label: Limited Fate
positions.summary: Some things are fated, but humans can influence details within bounds
positions.key_argument: Oracles show fixed outcomes, but the path to them admits variation

corpus_verdict: Fate dominates in religious and literary texts; philosophy increasingly questions absolute determinism
temporal_trend: Limited fate grows from 15% (Classical) to 30% (Imperial) as philosophical sophistication increases
genre_effect: Tragedy emphasizes absolute fate; philosophy questions it; historiography shows mixed causation

question: Is the soul material or immaterial?

positions.label: Material Soul
positions.summary: The soul is composed of fine material atoms or pneuma
positions.key_argument: Soul affects body and vice versa; only material can interact with material

positions.label: Immaterial Soul
positions.summary: The soul is purely spiritual substance distinct from matter
positions.key_argument: Soul's ability to grasp eternal forms proves its immaterial nature

positions.label: Soul as Harmony
positions.summary: Soul is the harmonious arrangement of bodily elements
positions.key_argument: Just as musical harmony emerges from but transcends individual notes

corpus_verdict: Material soul dominates in natural philosophy; immaterial soul in metaphysical contexts
temporal_trend: Immaterial view grows from 25% (Presocratic) to 45% (Neoplatonic) as metaphysics develops
genre_effect: Natural philosophy tends materialist; metaphysics and religion favor immaterial soul
